expectedText:
NOTICE TO PAY RENT OR QUIT
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

NOTICE DETAILS
NOTICE TO PAY RENT OR QUIT. To: Jordan Lee. Property: 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814. Date of this notice: September 1, 2026. Pat Morgan, as landlord, states that rent in the amount of $3,500 is now due and unpaid for the property described above. Within three (3) days after service of this notice, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and other judicial holidays, Jordan Lee must pay the full amount stated above or deliver possession of the property. Failure to do either within that period may result in legal proceedings to recover possession of the property.

THE THREE-DAY NOTICE: HOW THE PERIOD IS COUNTED
Under California statute, a tenant is guilty of unlawful detainer when the tenant continues in possession, without the landlord's permission, after default in payment of rent due under the lease, and the landlord has served a written three-day notice requiring payment of the rent or possession of the property, stating the amount due. The three days are counted excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and other judicial holidays — so a notice served on a Friday does not expire until the following Wednesday at the earliest (assuming no intervening holiday), not the following Monday. The notice may be served at any time within one year after the rent becomes due.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "When the tenant continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, without the permission of the landlord, or the successor in estate of the landlord, if applicable, after default in the payment of rent, pursuant to the lease or agreement under which the property is held, and three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due... or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon the subtenant."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(2), California Code of Civil Procedure, the three-day notice requirement and weekend/holiday exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  "The notice may be served at any time within one year after the rent becomes due."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(2) [one-year window], California Code of Civil Procedure, the one-year window for serving the notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  Known gap: This is California's statutory rule (Code of Civil Procedure section 1161, paragraph 2), not a rule that applies in every state — eviction notice periods, and how they are counted, vary by state, and some states count all calendar days rather than excluding weekends and holidays. This document addresses California's statewide statute only; it does not cover any city or county's local rent-control or eviction ordinance, and many California cities (San Francisco, Los Angeles, Oakland, and others) layer their own, often stricter, notice and just-cause requirements on top of this statewide floor. The "excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays" counting method was added to this paragraph by legislation effective September 1, 2019, replacing a rule that had counted all calendar days; that counting method remains in the statute's text as most recently amended, effective February 1, 2025, confirming it is still the operative rule as of the date this research was checked. The one-year service window and the three-day countdown are two distinct time limits within the same statutory paragraph, not independent sources, and are disclosed together here for that reason.

REQUIRED CONTENTS OF THE NOTICE
California's unlawful-detainer statute specifies what a three-day notice for nonpayment of rent must state: the amount of rent that is due, and the name, telephone number, and address of the person to whom the rent payment should be made. If payment may be made in person, the notice must also state the usual days and hours that person will be available to receive it. The statute additionally allows the notice to identify a financial-institution account (if the institution is within five miles of the rental property) or an electronic-funds-transfer procedure, if one is already established, as an alternative way to pay. California courts have held that a three-day notice under this statute is valid only if it strictly complies with these statutory requirements, and that a notice demanding more rent than is actually owed is defective.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due, the name, telephone number, and address of the person to whom the rent payment shall be made, and, if payment may be made personally, the usual days and hours that person will be available to receive the payment (provided that, if the address does not allow for personal delivery, then it shall be conclusively presumed that upon the mailing of any rent or notice to the owner by the tenant to the name and address provided, the notice or rent is deemed received by the owner on the date posted, if the tenant can show proof of mailing to the name and address provided by the owner), or the number of an account in a financial institution into which the rental payment may be made, and the name and street address of the institution (provided that the institution is located within five miles of the rental property), or if an electronic funds transfer procedure has been previously established, that payment may be made pursuant to that procedure, or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon the subtenant."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(2), California Code of Civil Procedure, the statutory content requirements for the notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  "An unlawful detainer action is not based upon contract...; it is a statutory proceeding and is governed solely by the provisions of the statute creating it... a lessor's action to recover possession of real property is not one for unlawful detainer where he does not comply with the statutory notice requirements"
  — Kwok v. Bergren, 130 Cal. App. 3d 596, 599-600 (1982) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2108681/kwok-v-bergren/)
  Known gap: This is California's statutory content checklist (Code of Civil Procedure section 1161, paragraph 2) and California case law construing it; both apply only to a tenancy governed by California law, and the specific items a notice must contain to be valid vary by state. This document covers the statewide requirement only — it does not address any additional content a specific city or county ordinance might require. The "strict compliance" rule quoted below comes from a published California Court of Appeal decision (Kwok v. Bergren, 1982), an independent source from the statute itself, not merely a different subsection of section 1161.

HOW THE NOTICE MAY BE SERVED
California statute prescribes three permitted methods for serving this notice on a residential tenant, to be used in this order of preference: (1) personal delivery to the tenant; (2) if the tenant cannot be found at home or at their usual place of business, leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at either place and also mailing a copy to the tenant's residence; or (3) if neither the tenant's residence nor place of business can be determined, or no person of suitable age or discretion can be found there, posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property and mailing a copy to the property address — commonly called "nail and mail" — while also handing a copy to anyone else found residing there. If a subtenant is in actual occupation of the property, service must also be made on the subtenant.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), the notices required by Sections 1161 and 1161a may be served by any of the following methods: (1) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (2) If he or she is absent from his or her place of residence, and from his or her usual place of business, by leaving a copy with some person of suitable age and discretion at either place, and sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at his or her place of residence. (3) If such place of residence and business cannot be ascertained, or a person of suitable age or discretion there can not be found, then by affixing a copy in a conspicuous place on the property, and also delivering a copy to a person there residing, if such person can be found; and also sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at the place where the property is situated. Service upon a subtenant may be made in the same manner."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1162(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, the permitted methods of serving the notice on a residential tenant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1162.)
  Known gap: This is California's statutory list of proper service methods (Code of Civil Procedure section 1162(a)) for the notice described elsewhere in this document; other states authorize different service methods, and some require methods this statute does not (such as certified mail alone). This document addresses the statewide method only — some California cities impose additional local service or documentation requirements on top of it. The statute also sets out a separate set of service methods for a commercial tenant, in a different subdivision of this same section, which this document does not address because it concerns residential tenancies. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1162(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

THE TENANT'S RIGHT TO PAY AND AVOID EVICTION
The three-day notice is written, by statute, as a choice: it requires "its payment... or possession of the property." A tenant who pays the full amount the notice states is due, within the three-day period, has complied with the notice, and the nonpayment ground for unlawful detainer described in the statute does not arise. In the neighboring paragraph of the same statute, covering a tenant's failure to perform other lease conditions or covenants, the Legislature has spelled this principle out expressly: within the three-day period, the tenant "may perform the conditions or covenants of the lease or pay the stipulated rent, as the case may be, and thereby save the lease from forfeiture."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due... or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(2), California Code of Civil Procedure, the notice's payment-or-possession structure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  "Within three days, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, after the service of the notice, the tenant, or any subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, or any mortgagee of the term, or other person interested in its continuance, may perform the conditions or covenants of the lease or pay the stipulated rent, as the case may be, and thereby save the lease from forfeiture; provided, if the conditions and covenants of the lease, violated by the lessee, cannot afterward be performed, then no notice, as last prescribed herein, need be given to the lessee or the subtenant, demanding the performance of the violated conditions or covenants of the lease."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(3), California Code of Civil Procedure, the express statutory cure-and-save-from-forfeiture language (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  Known gap: This is California statute (Code of Civil Procedure section 1161); the cure period, and whether curing avoids eviction at all, both vary by state. This document addresses California's statewide rule only, not any city or county's local ordinance. Both citations below come from the same statutory section — paragraph (2), covering rent default, and paragraph (3), covering other lease-covenant defaults — rather than independent sources; no additional independent source was found. Notably, the express "save the lease from forfeiture" sentence, quoted above, appears in paragraph (3)'s text governing other covenant breaches, not paragraph (2)'s rent-default text; paragraph (3)'s own wording nonetheless refers to a tenant choosing to "pay the stipulated rent... as the case may be" as one of the two ways to avoid forfeiture, so the same underlying principle — timely payment defeats the unlawful detainer claim — is expressed in both places, just not in identical sentences. This document states that structural fact rather than treating the two paragraphs as saying exactly the same thing.

NONPAYMENT OF RENT UNDER CALIFORNIA'S STATEWIDE JUST-CAUSE LAW
Since 2020, California's Tenant Protection Act has required a landlord to have "just cause," stated in the written termination notice, to end certain tenancies once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months (or, in some multi-tenant situations, 24 months). Default in the payment of rent is specifically listed in the statute as one form of "at-fault just cause." Unlike some other at-fault violations under this law, a landlord is not required to give a separate advance notice-and-cure step before serving a nonpayment three-day notice — the three-day pay-or-quit notice described elsewhere in this document is itself the notice the statute contemplates for a rent default. The Tenant Protection Act's just-cause requirement does not apply to every California tenancy: the statute lists a number of specific exemptions, including (among others) certain single-family owner-occupied residences, certain small two-unit owner-occupied properties, housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, and housing meeting specified individually-alienable-title and non-corporate-ownership conditions paired with a required written exemption notice to the tenant. This statewide just-cause requirement is currently scheduled to expire, and be repealed, on January 1, 2030.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(a), California Civil Code, the statewide just-cause requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.2.)
  "For purposes of this section, 'just cause' means either of the following: (1) At-fault just cause, which means any of the following: (A) Default in the payment of rent."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(b)(1)(A), California Civil Code, nonpayment of rent as at-fault just cause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.2.)
  "Before an owner of residential real property issues a notice to terminate a tenancy for just cause that is a curable lease violation, the owner shall first give notice of the violation to the tenant with an opportunity to cure the violation pursuant to paragraph (3) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(c), California Civil Code, the separate cure-notice step that applies to other curable lease violations but not to a rent default (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.2.)
  "This section shall not apply to the following types of residential real properties or residential circumstances: (1) Transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1940. (2) Housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly... or an adult residential facility... (3) Dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or a kindergarten and grades 1 to 12, inclusive, school. (4) Housing accommodations in which the tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with the owner who maintains their principal residence at the residential real property. (5) Single-family owner-occupied residences, including both of the following: (A) A residence in which the owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms... (B) A mobilehome. (6) A property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in which the owner occupied one of the units as the owner's principal place of residence at the beginning of the tenancy, so long as the owner continues in occupancy... (7) Housing that has been issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless the housing is a mobilehome. (8) Residential real property, including a mobilehome, that is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit, provided that both of the following apply: (A) The owner is not any of the following: (i) A real estate investment trust... (ii) A corporation. (iii) A limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation. (iv) Management of a mobilehome park... (B) The tenants have been provided written notice that the residential property is exempt from this section... (9) Housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement with a government agency, or other recorded document as affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income..."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(e), California Civil Code, the just-cause law's stated exemptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.2.)
  "This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2030, and as of that date is repealed."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(n), California Civil Code, the just-cause law's own sunset date (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.2.)
  Known gap: This is a California statewide statute (Civil Code section 1946.2), not a rule that exists in every state, and the exemption list above is a summary, not a complete restatement — the statute's exemption paragraph runs to nine numbered categories with detailed sub-conditions attached to several of them (for example, the single-family and small-property exemptions carry specific occupancy and unit-count conditions, and the individually-alienable-title exemption requires a specific written notice using statutory language), and this document does not attempt to reproduce every condition. A related statute, Civil Code section 1947.12, caps how much rent can be increased over a 12-month period for many of the same tenancies; it governs rent increases, not the eviction-notice process, so it is not reproduced here, but it exists alongside the just-cause rule as part of the same legislative package. This document addresses statewide California law only; a number of California cities and counties have their own local rent-control and just-cause ordinances that impose additional or different requirements on top of the statewide law, and this document does not cover any of them. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1946.2) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was used for this clause.

COVID-19-ERA NOTICE MODIFICATIONS: CURRENT STATUS
California enacted temporary COVID-19-era eviction protections beginning in 2020, including a period during which nonpayment notices for COVID-19 rental debt required a longer notice period and specific tenant-facing declarations rather than the standard three-day notice. Those temporary statutes carried their own expiration dates. As of the date this document's sourcing was checked, no COVID-19-era modification to the notice period or notice contents remains in the currently codified text governing this notice: the operative statute is the version of Code of Civil Procedure section 1161 most recently amended effective February 1, 2025, and its text imposes the standard three-day (weekend/holiday-excluded) notice period described elsewhere in this document, with no COVID-19-related exception or extended period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(Amended (as added by Stats. 2020, Ch. 37, Sec. 16) by Stats. 2024, Ch. 287, Sec. 6. (SB 611) Effective January 1, 2025. Operative February 1, 2025, by its own provisions.)"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(2), California Code of Civil Procedure, current operative text and amendment history showing no COVID-19-era modification remains (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  Known gap: This is a currency check against California's currently codified statute, not a claim that no COVID-19-related eviction rule was ever adopted anywhere — other states and some California cities may have adopted their own, separate protections on different timelines, and this document does not track those. The finding here rests on direct review of the current text of the statute that would carry any such modification if one still applied (Code of Civil Procedure section 1161), which contains no COVID-19-related provision; direct lookups of the specific code sections that had carried California's now-expired COVID-19 tenant relief provisions (Code of Civil Procedure section 1179.01 and a related Civil Code section in the 1179 series, added in 2020) returned no codified text at those citations, consistent with those provisions having sunset and been removed from the code rather than merely amended. This is reported as a negative finding based on direct source review, not a claim independently verified against a repealing bill's legislative history. This is a single statutory citation (§ 1161); no additional independent source was found for this.

PAYMENT INSTRUCTIONS
Rent payment under this notice should be made to: Acme Properties, LLC, telephone (555) 123-4567, at 123 Main St, Suite 100, Sacramento, CA 95814. If payment may be made in person, the usual days and hours available to receive payment are: Monday-Friday, 9am-5pm. Payment may also be made by any other method the parties have previously and separately agreed to in writing, including an established electronic funds transfer procedure or a designated financial institution account.

LANDLORD SIGNATURE AND DECLARATION OF SERVICE
Signed: Pat Morgan, Landlord. Date: _______________.

Declaration of Service. This notice was served on Jordan Lee on _______________ (date), by the following method (check one): ☐ personal delivery to the tenant; ☐ leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the tenant's residence or usual place of business, together with mailing a copy to the tenant's residence; ☐ posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property and mailing a copy to the property address, after the tenant's residence and place of business could not be ascertained or no person of suitable age or discretion could be found there.

Served by: _______________ (name) Date: _______________

Default in the payment of rent is specifically listed in the statute as one form of "at-fault just cause." Unlike some other at-fault violations under this law, a landlord is not required to give a separate advance notice-and-cure step before serving a nonpayment three-day notice — the three-day pay-or-quit notice described elsewhere in this document is itself the notice the statute contemplates for a rent default. The Tenant Protection Act's just-cause requirement does not apply to every California tenancy: the statute lists a number of specific exemptions, including (among others) certain single-family owner-occupied residences, certain small two-unit owner-occupied properties, housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, and housing meeting specified individually-alienable-title and non-corporate-ownership conditions paired with a required written exemption notice to the tenant. This statewide just-cause requirement is currently scheduled to expire, and be repealed, on January 1, 2030.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the statewide just-cause requirement
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, nonpayment of rent as at-fault just cause
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, 'just cause' means either of the following: (1) At-fault just cause, which means any of the following: (A) Default in the payment of rent.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the separate cure-notice step that applies to other curable lease violations but not to a rent default
citations.quote: Before an owner of residential real property issues a notice to terminate a tenancy for just cause that is a curable lease violation, the owner shall first give notice of the violation to the tenant with an opportunity to cure the violation pursuant to paragraph (3) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the just-cause law's stated exemptions
citations.quote: This section shall not apply to the following types of residential real properties or residential circumstances: (1) Transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1940. (2) Housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly... or an adult residential facility... (3) Dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or a kindergarten and grades 1 to 12, inclusive, school. (4) Housing accommodations in which the tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with the owner who maintains their principal residence at the residential real property. (5) Single-family owner-occupied residences, including both of the following: (A) A residence in which the owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms... (B) A mobilehome. (6) A property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in which the owner occupied one of the units as the owner's principal place of residence at the beginning of the tenancy, so long as the owner continues in occupancy... (7) Housing that has been issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless the housing is a mobilehome. (8) Residential real property, including a mobilehome, that is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit, provided that both of the following apply: (A) The owner is not any of the following: (i) A real estate investment trust... (ii) A corporation. (iii) A limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation. (iv) Management of a mobilehome park... (B) The tenants have been provided written notice that the residential property is exempt from this section... (9) Housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement with a government agency, or other recorded document as affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income...

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the just-cause law's own sunset date
citations.quote: This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2030, and as of that date is repealed.

expectedJSON.gap: This is a California statewide statute (Civil Code section 1946.2), not a rule that exists in every state, and the exemption list above is a summary, not a complete restatement — the statute's exemption paragraph runs to nine numbered categories with detailed sub-conditions attached to several of them (for example, the single-family and small-property exemptions carry specific occupancy and unit-count conditions, and the individually-alienable-title exemption requires a specific written notice using statutory language), and this document does not attempt to reproduce every condition. A related statute, Civil Code section 1947.12, caps how much rent can be increased over a 12-month period for many of the same tenancies; it governs rent increases, not the eviction-notice process, so it is not reproduced here, but it exists alongside the just-cause rule as part of the same legislative package. This document addresses statewide California law only; a number of California cities and counties have their own local rent-control and just-cause ordinances that impose additional or different requirements on top of the statewide law, and this document does not cover any of them. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1946.2) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was used for this clause.

expectedJSON.body: California enacted temporary COVID-19-era eviction protections beginning in 2020, including a period during which nonpayment notices for COVID-19 rental debt required a longer notice period and specific tenant-facing declarations rather than the standard three-day notice. Those temporary statutes carried their own expiration dates. As of the date this document's sourcing was checked, no COVID-19-era modification to the notice period or notice contents remains in the currently codified text governing this notice: the operative statute is the version of Code of Civil Procedure section 1161 most recently amended effective February 1, 2025, and its text imposes the standard three-day (weekend/holiday-excluded) notice period described elsewhere in this document, with no COVID-19-related exception or extended period.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, current operative text and amendment history showing no COVID-19-era modification remains
citations.quote: (Amended (as added by Stats. 2020, Ch. 37, Sec. 16) by Stats. 2024, Ch. 287, Sec. 6. (SB 611) Effective January 1, 2025. Operative February 1, 2025, by its own provisions.)

expectedJSON.gap: This is a currency check against California's currently codified statute, not a claim that no COVID-19-related eviction rule was ever adopted anywhere — other states and some California cities may have adopted their own, separate protections on different timelines, and this document does not track those. The finding here rests on direct review of the current text of the statute that would carry any such modification if one still applied (Code of Civil Procedure section 1161), which contains no COVID-19-related provision; direct lookups of the specific code sections that had carried California's now-expired COVID-19 tenant relief provisions (Code of Civil Procedure section 1179.01 and a related Civil Code section in the 1179 series, added in 2020) returned no codified text at those citations, consistent with those provisions having sunset and been removed from the code rather than merely amended. This is reported as a negative finding based on direct source review, not a claim independently verified against a repealing bill's legislative history. This is a single statutory citation (§ 1161); no additional independent source was found for this.
